title: Stop Living a B+ Life: How to Find the Life You Actually Want | Dr. Suzy Welch
guest: Dr. Suzy Welch, NYU Stern professor, former Harvard Business Review editor-in-chief, author of Becoming You and creator of the Values Bridge
summary: Director's cut of the hosts' interview with Suzy Welch: she walks Cherie and Jean through their Values Bridge results (16 rank-ordered values and the 'authenticity gap' between holding and living them), then shares money, love and reinvention lessons including 'there is no last best deal', cutting sunk-cost losses, and 'maybe he's right' as a marriage technique. In the BTS debrief the sisters reflect on confronting yourself with an objective tool, the 'swag gap' in dating, abundance vs scarcity mindset, and Cherie's mantra DILMO (do it, learn, move on).

ideas.idea: Answering 'what should I do with my life' requires excavating three data sets: your values, your aptitudes, and your economically viable interests.
ideas.detail: Welch's Becoming You course (800 students on the waitlist in one semester) synthesizes all three into purpose; knowing your values alone is not enough because you could want to be Celine Dion and have a bad voice.

ideas.idea: The Values Bridge rank-orders your 16 values and measures the 'authenticity gap' between how much you hold each value and how much you are actually living it.
ideas.detail: Built with a team of engineers and psychometricians as the basis of Welch's PhD; about 65-66,000 people took it in the first weeks after its May 6 release. The hosts say it gives you a vocabulary to name things you already felt.
names_or_cases: Wittgenstein: 'the limits of my language are the limits of my world'

ideas.idea: No value is good or bad; values are choices with consequences and the tool lets people talk about them without judgment.
ideas.detail: Welch has eudaimonia at 15 of 16 and says her joy is in work and achievement; Jean was embarrassed that beholderism was her number one until Welch reframed it as a common value that is also one of her own top values.

ideas.idea: Partners need to share strongly presenting values like radius (desire for systemic change) and belovedness, or the relationship will be a constant fight about priorities.
ideas.detail: The test gives couples a conflict/harmony score; Welch's daughter and fiance had identical top six values. Cherie recalls an ex in her 20s who wanted a plain house in the suburbs while she dreamed of impact, which Welch calls a near-100% conflict.

ideas.idea: Achievement (wanting success others can see) is only the number 11 value for Gen Z but ranks high for business school types, which is why both sisters have it in their top four.
ideas.detail: Cherie has achievement at number 2 and Jean at number 4; Welch says business schools select for it and Gen Z students ask 'who needs that'.

ideas.idea: Eudaimonia (self-care, recreation, pleasure) typically conflicts with affluence and achievement, which explains the 'oh' feeling many young people get when they want both.
ideas.detail: Many students rank eudaimonia first with affluence or achievement right behind it; those values do not track together unless you inherited wealth. Jean says finance culture taught her to put self-care aside to succeed.

ideas.idea: If your values mismatch your organization's culture you go to work every day 'in a suit three sizes too small', so use your values to test whether you will last somewhere.
ideas.detail: People with very high voice (authentic self-expression) will find Goldman Sachs a poor fit, while high-achievement, high-affluence, low-voice people go into investment banking and don't mind. Young women often have voice ranked first with a 98% authenticity gap.

ideas.idea: Beholderism, caring how things look including yourself, is often a proxy for wanting harmony and control over the one thing you can control: your environment.
ideas.detail: It is the top value for almost every influencer Welch has worked with; Jean read dozens of interior design books at age 12 and rearranges flowers that clash with a room. Welch advises Jean to check a future partner's beholderism because it bumps into restaurants, houses and vacations.

ideas.idea: Belovedness, the desire for an intimate partner relationship, often shows up as a top value with a huge gap for women who have been told to 'girlboss' their careers.
ideas.detail: Welch sees women with belovedness at number one and a 98% gap who never felt able to say they also want marriage. She recommends both partners have belovedness in the same tier (both top five or both bottom five).

ideas.idea: Values are fairly stable from about age 25, but seismic life events like a death, divorce or having a child can reorder them, so results are a snapshot in time.
ideas.detail: Jean's belovedness dropped to 11 after breaking an eight-year engagement in which she thinks she over-expressed it; Welch's own belovedness went to 16 after her husband Jack died. The hosts plan to retake the test yearly to track the gap.

ideas.idea: Four 'horsemen of dream destruction', all starting with E, pull people off their own lives: expectations, experience (the easy path), events, and economic security.
ideas.detail: Examples: taking the job your neighbor's brother can offer because it is easy, or staying in something after a layoff. Welch offers a free quiz to identify which horseman is taking your life; for Gen Z stability (the 'scope' value) matters more than affluence.

ideas.idea: People habitually live B or B+ lives for decades, and it usually takes a crisis like being fired, divorced or dumped to force the self-examination; do the work before the crisis.
ideas.detail: The outside world confirms your life looks like an A while you know inside it is not; Jean says her seemingly perfect couple and high-powered job was a B+ life she is now grateful crashed. Welch: you would otherwise be 45, crying in your car asking 'what have I done'.

ideas.idea: There is no universal work-life 'balance'; figure out what YOUR balance is and give yourself permission to live it.
ideas.detail: Welch cites Jensen Huang saying 'I love my work-life balance, I work all the time'; rank ordering lets people admit they want fame, money and achievement with eudaimonia at the bottom and stop lying about it.

ideas.idea: 'There is no last best deal': sellers, realtors and stock promoters manufacture urgency, and remembering another deal always comes prevents stupid purchases.
ideas.detail: Welch says this saved her many wrong turns, especially in real estate. The hosts adopted it as a mantra and extend it to relationships, since believing someone is the last best deal is how you settle; Welch's 55-year-old friend stayed with a terrible partner because 'who else is there'.

ideas.idea: Fight the sunk cost fallacy: when you have made a financial, job or relationship mistake, own it publicly, take the hit and get out now.
ideas.detail: Welch sold a house she had fixed up after two years because it was the wrong place, despite friends' objections. Decision science shows we are wired to pour more money on problems to save face; people respect you more for cutting losses, not less.

ideas.idea: Treat your mistakes as 'the wisdom project': wisdom comes from what you did wrong, not what you did right.
ideas.detail: Welch says she gathered her wisdom from a long list of mistakes; the hosts connect this to Cherie's mantra DILMO, 'do it, learn, move on', invented around age 22, where moving on is the hardest part.

ideas.idea: A dual-career marriage worked because the partners shared values, talked constantly, and respected each other's lanes of expertise.
ideas.detail: Welch was never CEO of GE managing 400,000 people and Jack never wrote or edited books; he had very high agency and she very low, and she thinks two high-agency partners would have been a different story.

ideas.idea: When your partner says something you disagree with, silently assume 'maybe he's right' and hear them out non-defensively before stating where you differ.
ideas.detail: Welch started from the supposition that Jack loved her, trusted him and wanted the best for the marriage; sometimes he was right, and other times her openness let her explain her view so he'd say 'I never thought of that'. The hosts note this takes immense self-regulation.

ideas.idea: Assuming good intent can change the trajectory of your life and career; you occasionally get burned, but far more often you gain relationships you'd never have had.
ideas.detail: Jack Welch went to parties of strangers saying 'could anything be more exciting', treating everyone as a friend he hadn't met yet.

ideas.idea: Reinvention comes with the territory because the economy, the world and you keep changing; you can 'die a thousand times' in a career and be reborn.
ideas.detail: Welch was fired from Harvard Business Review in her 40s, reported in the Wall Street Journal, refused a press release saying she resigned, and two weeks later Oprah's organization called. She started on manual typewriters, was an early BlackBerry adopter, and got her PhD in her 60s.

ideas.idea: Building something that changes people's lives is an addictive flow state, and after losing a spouse there is a fearlessness because nothing can scare you anymore.
ideas.detail: Welch gets daily DMs saying the Values Bridge changed someone's life and tells her kids 'I'm building something' when they say take a break; she also went on her first date six years after Jack died and found she referenced him 30 times.

ideas.idea: Confronting yourself with an objective tool is painful but the most revealing thing you can do, and accepting every part of yourself makes you more successful and happier.
ideas.detail: The hosts value that the test is science-based, unlike Myers-Briggs or Enneagram, and that it asks 'whose life did I just live', a question that scares Cherie into looking at her authenticity score honestly. Cherie's gap on her top five values was low, which felt affirming.

ideas.idea: The 'swag gap' is real: a couple with very different levels of beholderism struggles to coexist even if they look perfect on paper.
ideas.detail: Jean ended things with a man who later sent her a Wall Street Journal article on the swag gap; she wishes credentials on paper could capture someone's love of art and aesthetics. The hosts say everyone judges a book by its cover in how you show up.
names_or_cases: Codie Sanchez (women who wear makeup make 30% more)

ideas.idea: How you present yourself matters and is within your control, so refuse to be written off for something you can manage.
ideas.detail: Jean wishes she had invested more in presentation earlier; being on camera makes it more important than ever, and they cite Codie Sanchez's 'paint me up like a clown, I'll make more money'. The hosts acknowledge the standards differ for men and women.

ideas.idea: Abundance mindset comes from having abundance: earlier desperation (needing a job to pay student loans) was rational, and now being in a good place lets you choose partners and brands.
ideas.detail: Cherie says she didn't have the privilege of an abundance mindset when she graduated with loans; Jean says holding too tightly to 'the only chance' is scarcity mindset she held onto too long.
